guides.title: Ivermectin
guides.description: An antiparasitic with negative randomized COVID-19 findings and laboratory cancer research.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Ivermectin is an oral antiparasitic medicine in the avermectin class. Its U.S. tablet label covers intestinal strongyloidiasis, caused by Strongyloides stercoralis, and onchocerciasis, caused by Onchocerca volvulus. These established parasite indications are separate from the COVID-19 and cancer investigations discussed here. The six-day higher-dose ACTIV-6 trial did not shorten sustained recovery in outpatients with COVID-19, and COVID-OUT did not demonstrate a reduction in its primary composite outcome with ivermectin. Cancer experiments have examined ovarian cancer cells, glioblastoma models, breast cancer models and WNT-TCF-dependent colorectal tumors. Those experiments address biological mechanisms and tumor growth in laboratory systems; they do not establish improved survival, symptoms or quality of life for people with cancer. The cited liver-cancer combination report is retracted and excluded from efficacy conclusions.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Six days of higher-dose ivermectin did not improve sustained recovery from acute COVID-19. Ovarian, brain, breast and colorectal cancer experiments reported effects in cells or animals, without a patient benefit estimate from those experiments. The liver-cancer combination report is retracted and excluded from efficacy conclusions.

questions.answer: No significant improvement in sustained recovery was found in the six-day ACTIV-6 trial.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: The oral label reports dizziness, gastrointestinal symptoms, itching and rash in studies of intestinal strongyloidiasis. In onchocerciasis, inflammatory reactions to dying microfilariae can cause fever, skin symptoms, lymph-node tenderness and eye reactions; the disease and the treatment context affect how these events are interpreted. Postmarketing reports include low blood pressure, seizures, serious skin reactions and liver injury. The label also warns about neurotoxicity, including confusion, impaired consciousness and coma, which has been reported with recommended dosing as well as overdose. Heavy Loa loa infection creates a separate risk of severe or fatal encephalopathy; significant exposure in endemic parts of West or Central Africa calls for assessment before treatment. These label warnings apply independently of whether a repurposing experiment reports an interesting pathway effect.

questions.question: Why does Loa loa exposure matter?
questions.answer: The label describes severe or fatal encephalopathy in heavily infected patients and calls for pretreatment assessment after significant exposure in endemic areas of West or Central Africa. Neurotoxicity has also been reported without Loa loa infection.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: Hypersensitivity to any component of the oral product is the label’s formal contraindication. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, low body weight and possible Loa loa exposure are addressed separately under precautions, rather than being interchangeable with that formal contraindication. The suitability table separates these situations so that a trial exclusion or a precaution is not presented as a universal prohibition.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: The oral label describes rare postmarketing reports of increased INR when ivermectin was given with warfarin. INR is a measure used to monitor warfarin anticoagulation; this reported interaction is a reason for medication review, rather than evidence that every combination has been tested. The label identifies CYP3A4 as the main enzyme involved in ivermectin metabolism in laboratory studies, but that observation alone does not quantify the clinical effect of every CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer. A complete interaction assessment for experimental cancer combinations is not on hand in the cited sources.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: Labeled dosing depends on the parasite indication and body weight: the oral label describes approximately 200 micrograms/kg as a single dose for intestinal strongyloidiasis and approximately 150 micrograms/kg as a single dose for onchocerciasis. The tablets are taken with water on an empty stomach, and follow-up is part of the labeled treatment context. ACTIV-6 instead tested a maximum target of 600 micrograms/kg daily for six days in outpatients with COVID-19; that research schedule did not improve sustained recovery. An experimental schedule is not an established dose for another disease, and the cited cancer experiments do not establish a human cancer-treatment regimen.

questions.question: What follow-up does the oral label describe?
questions.answer: For intestinal strongyloidiasis, follow-up stool examinations verify parasite clearance. Onchocerciasis treatment does not kill adult parasites, so follow-up and retreatment are generally needed; the label describes retreatment intervals as short as three months for individual patients.

questions.question: Does the label establish dosing below 15 kg?
questions.answer: No. Safety and effectiveness in children weighing less than 15 kg have not been established. This is a missing pediatric evidence basis, not an experimental dose recommendation.

sections.label: Results
sections.paragraph: The negative recovery trial directly evaluated patients; the cancer mechanisms were measured in experimental systems.

sections.label: Quality
sections.paragraph: The cited U.S. label describes a human oral product supplied as 3 mg tablets. It also records human intoxication after exposure to veterinary ivermectin formulations, so the product and route cannot be treated as incidental details when interpreting safety. This page’s dosing and status descriptions refer to the labeled oral tablet, while the cancer studies describe experimental systems rather than an approved cancer formulation.

sections.label: Status
sections.paragraph: The US oral indications are parasitic infections; they do not include COVID-19 or cancer.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: The clinical and laboratory findings answer different questions. ACTIV-6 evaluated sustained recovery in people with acute COVID-19 and did not demonstrate a benefit from its six-day higher-dose schedule. COVID-OUT evaluated a primary composite of hypoxemia, emergency care, hospitalization or death; the existing ivermectin outcome assessment did not demonstrate a reduction. The colorectal-cancer study used pathway activation and comparison models to test whether WNT-TCF signaling contributed to the experimental growth effect. That mechanistic finding does not supply a clinical cancer-benefit estimate or an independent randomized patient trial. The table retains the existing outcome-specific benefit assessment and trial identities; it does not transfer metformin’s grades or count related reports as new trials. The retracted liver-cancer report remains visible only for source-integrity context and contributes no efficacy conclusion.

faqs.question: What is its established use?
faqs.answer: The cited oral tablet is approved for intestinal strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis. Those indications do not establish a COVID-19 or cancer indication.

faqs.question: Which adverse effects matter most?
faqs.answer: Reported harms include dizziness, low blood pressure, serious skin reactions and neurotoxicity; heavy Loa loa infection can increase the risk of severe encephalopathy.

originalAction.text: Ivermectin binds parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels, increasing chloride entry and causing paralysis and death of susceptible parasites.

sentences.text: Ivermectin binds parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels, increasing chloride entry and causing paralysis and death of susceptible parasites.

summary.text: Repurposing studies examine actions different from parasite killing. Ovarian and breast cancer experiments investigated PAK1-related growth signaling, while glioblastoma experiments examined mitochondrial respiration and oxidative stress. Colorectal-cancer experiments tested WNT-TCF-dependent growth using pathway rescue and comparison models. These are experimental mechanisms, not demonstrated patient benefits. The antiviral membrane experiments also raise an exposure limitation: their effects occurred at concentrations above reported toxic clinical concentrations.

questions.title: Why did ivermectin attract COVID-19 research?
questions.text: Cell-culture antiviral activity prompted trials; later experiments linked this activity to membrane disruption at concentrations above reported toxic clinical concentrations.

questions.text: Ivermectin inhibited PAK1, a growth-signaling kinase, and suppressed growth of ovarian cancer cell lines.

questions.title: Testing the WNT–TCF explanation
questions.text: In colorectal-cancer experiments, forcing TCF signaling back on rescued cells from some low-concentration ivermectin effects. Ivermectin also inhibited TCF-dependent mouse xenografts but not a TCF-independent comparison model. This is stronger mechanistic evidence than an association between a pathway marker and cell death. Its relevance still depends on tumor biology, exposure and formulation; it does not establish clinical cancer benefit.
